title: Kincaid scouts the San Juans for a station site
summary: UW zoologist Trevor Kincaid toured the San Juan Islands by small boat looking for a base for summer marine fieldwork. He chose Friday Harbor over Port Townsend and a Kitsap County bay, judging that the islands' variety of sea life was worth the distance. FHL's newsletters and UW's student paper now date the Labs from 1903, although the first summer session was held in 1904 and UW marked the centennial in 2004.

title: A lab site is chosen and a summer school announced
summary: In January 1904 Kincaid returned to Friday Harbor to pick a laboratory site, most likely a point near the harbor's eastern entrance; without buildings, the first season was to be held to about 25 people. In March the university announced that its summer botany and zoology fieldwork would move there, with science teachers given priority and a launch and dredges for surveying Puget Sound.

title: The first summer session
summary: In about mid-June 1904 (the station diary gives June 15), Kincaid and botanist Theodore C. Frye brought a dozen or more teachers and students to camp in tents next to a cabin that Captain Edward Warbass had lent them south of town. There were no formal classes: the group spent six weeks collecting on shore and dredging around the islands, and when the session closed on July 29 the students urged UW to invite other schools to form a Northwest school of biology.

title: Second season: Frye in charge, working from a cannery
summary: With Kincaid on leave at Harvard, Frye ran the June 19 to July 29 session from the Pacific American Fisheries cannery and wharf on the town waterfront. The local paper reported that the cannery had been secured for 1905, although later histories date the cannery years from 1906. The group chartered the shrimp steamer Zebeitka to dredge deep water and began what was described as a biological survey of Puget Sound, including a study of local shrimp.

title: Town and lab: a school collection and an open house
summary: The Friday Harbor school board arranged for its principal, F. F. Joubert, to attend the 1905 session and build a marine collection for the town school; by early August he had gathered about 200 specimens. On the evening of July 21 the lab opened to visitors, and many came to see the work and the collections. Public open houses turn up again in 1929 and the mid-1930s, and FHL now holds one every spring.

title: Classes in the cannery; Kincaid calls for a permanent lab
summary: With Kincaid back in charge in 1906, the session offered classes in marine zoology and botany centered on classification and anatomy, and his dredging yielded about forty species, one of them new to science. He returned to Seattle in August hoping the legislature would fund a permanent laboratory at Friday Harbor like the one at Woods Hole.

title: Eyes on the Point Caution military reserve
summary: During a short visit in 1907, Kincaid said he hoped to put a marine station on the Point Caution military reserve at Friday Harbor, and in 1908 he began lobbying Washington's members of Congress for the land. In January 1909 the state legislature formally asked the federal government to give part of the reserve to the state for a permanent university station, but it took twelve more years to obtain.

title: Fourth session: Frye recruits widely
summary: Frye ran the 1907 session (June 24 to August 2) with zoologist Charles W. Prentiss and invited scientists and students from many institutions. Plant ecologist Henry C. Cowles of the University of Chicago lectured while his party stopped for a week on its way to Alaska. In July about 150 townspeople and station members held a picnic together at Point Caution to mark the school's fourth summer in Friday Harbor.

title: A town picnic for the biologists
summary: The San Juan Islander announced a public picnic in honour of the university summer school of biology, to show local interest in the work done at Friday Harbor for four years under Kincaid and Frye. It was planned near Point Caution on the military reserve, with free transport, or at the cannery buildings in bad weather. A week later the paper reported that it was largely attended.

title: Fifth session: a summer school for teachers
summary: The fifth annual session opened in the cannery buildings on June 22, 1908, for six weeks of courses in animal ecology, zoology and botany, with a $13 fee and most students in tents. All twenty students were working teachers, about half of them from Iowa. Iowa botanist Robert B. Wylie and his Iowa students named a seaweed-rich rock on Lopez Island 'Iowa rock', and a chartered oyster-company steamer, the Crescent, replaced a smaller boat for the class's dredging.

title: Andrew Newhall's gift: land of the station's own
summary: The old cannery quarters went back to canning salmon, so UW officials chose waterfront land offered by Captain Andrew Newhall next to the 1904 campsite instead of the military reserve, which would have been slow to obtain. The Regents accepted the gift on April 26, 1909, and the legislature added $6,000 for buildings. Reports of the site's shoreline range from 200 to 400 feet, and UW President Thomas Kane promised that students from every institution would be welcome there.

title: Reorganized as the Puget Sound Marine Station
summary: In spring 1909 the station became the Puget Sound Marine Station, run by UW with the State College of Washington and the state normal schools at Bellingham, Cheney and Ellensburg under a seven-member board, with other colleges invited to join. Its backers wanted a shared regional laboratory modeled on Woods Hole.

title: A first season split between Friday Harbor and Olga
summary: The new station's first session opened at Friday Harbor on June 21, 1909, and moved halfway through to Olga on Orcas Island, with Whitman College biologist H. S. Brode as director. Nine courses and 27 evening lectures, many of them open to the public, drew 39 students, instructors and investigators from 13 states and two other countries. The split summer was unpopular, and after Governor Marion Hay declined to support two separate stations, UW kept Friday Harbor and the Olga site was abandoned in 1910.

title: Kincaid becomes the first official director
summary: Trevor Kincaid became the first official director of the Puget Sound Marine Station, advised by a council of faculty from several colleges while UW paid the operating costs. In the first season in the new buildings, seven courses were taught, a University of Kansas zoology party came for the summer, a work-boat was bought, and interest kept the station open nearly all summer; in August Kincaid told the Seattle Times the station could become a leading center for marine research.

title: The first laboratory rises over the water
summary: With $2,700 approved by the Regents in March, work began in April 1910 on a two-and-a-half-story laboratory set on concrete piers over the water, so that boats could unload right at the building. By July it had electric lights, running spring water and two large aquaria from Seattle's 1909 exposition. The much-remodeled building still stood on the Friday Harbor waterfront in the 2000s, known as Capron's Landing.

title: A dining and lecture hall above the lab
summary: In June and July 1911 a two-story hall went up just uphill from the lab, with a dining room on the ground floor and a lecture room with a large stone fireplace above, and it became the camp's social center and library. The Regents had bought three more acres that spring, and a family cottage, a float for unloading specimens and running fresh and salt water were added for a session of 64 students.

title: Tenth season: a city of tents
summary: Ten more tents went up for the tenth annual session. An early-July count found 108 people in camp, including 60 students from 18 colleges and schools, 35 of them women, and women also outnumbered men in later counts through 1917. The chartered steamer Violet took groups dredging and on trips to Mount Constitution and the Sucia Islands, and visiting Missouri zoologist W. C. Curtis predicted the station would in time become the country's greatest marine laboratory, urging the university to settle on a permanent site.

title: Botanist T. C. Frye becomes director
summary: Kincaid resigned because he found the multi-college governing council too hard to work with, and in March 1914 Theodore C. Frye, head of UW botany, was appointed director, a post he held until 1930. Under Frye the station aimed to bring students and investigators together, to give schoolteachers a lasting interest in biology, and to foster research.

title: A record summer for research
summary: Frye reported to UW President Henry Landes that the 1914 session, with 73 people including 43 regular students, had produced more research for publication than the station's previous ten years put together. Ecologist Victor E. Shelford of the University of Chicago was among the visiting faculty, and the station offered a course in marine animal ecology that summer.
people: T. C. Frye; Henry Landes; Victor E. Shelford

title: The station starts its own publication series
summary: Frye founded and edited Puget Sound Marine Station Publications to report research done at the station, including Nathan Fasten's work on crab reproduction and Walter Muenscher's 1917 key to the brown seaweeds of Puget Sound. The series took the station's new name in 1918 and ran to seven volumes, the last issue appearing in March 1931.
people: T. C. Frye; Nathan Fasten; Walter R. C. Muenscher

title: The first site proves too small
summary: Frye wrote to UW President Henry Suzzallo that the Newhall site was steep and muddy and had only 400 feet of shoreline, and that sewage and cannery waste fouled the water, so seawater had to be piped in from a distance. In September 1916 Suzzallo and a committee of regents inspected the station and reported that it would soon have to expand.
people: T. C. Frye; Henry Suzzallo; H. T. Condon

title: Regents ask for the Point Caution reserve
summary: The UW Regents formally asked the War Department to give the university the 484-acre Point Caution military tract on San Juan Island as a new home for the station. Getting it took an act of Congress and four more years.
sources: [{"title": "Mills & Hermans, FHL Historical Centennial Timeline (1917 entry)", "url": "https://faculty.washington.edu/cemills/FHLTimeline.html"}]

title: Renamed the Puget Sound Biological Station
summary: During World War I, about 1917-18, the station was renamed the Puget Sound Biological Station, because its name and mail were being confused with the Navy's marine station and yards on the Sound. By May 1918 notices for the six-week summer course used the new name, and the publication series carried it from volume 2 on.

title: The regents lease the Point Caution reserve
summary: W. T. Perkins, president of the Board of Regents, signed papers leasing 484 acres of the Point Caution military reserve on San Juan Island for a university biological research school, three years before Congress granted the land outright.
sources: [{"title": "The Seattle Star, August 3, 1918, p. 3, 'University Gets Biological Side' (Chronicling America)", "url": "https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn87093407/1918-08-03/ed-1/?sp=3"}]

title: Crowded out at the old site
summary: By 1920 about 150 students were camping on the steep hillside at the old site while a nearby cannery dumped its waste into the bay; the six-week term of classes, collecting trips by rowboat and evening talks around a bonfire cost $60. That September President Henry Suzzallo, other UW officials and Frye spent a week looking over the Point Caution reserve, the expected new home.
sources: [{"title": "Mills & Hermans, FHL Historical Centennial Timeline (1920 entries, citing Friday Harbor Journal)", "url": "https://faculty.washington.edu/cemills/FHLTimeline.html"}]

title: Congress grants the Point Caution land
summary: Regent William T. Perkins and Senator Miles Poindexter pressed the request in Congress, and President Warren G. Harding then signed an act giving UW the 484-acre Point Caution military reservation for a biological station and for general university research. It is still the Labs' home; a 2004 survey measured it at 476 acres.
people: Warren G. Harding; William T. Perkins; Miles Poindexter; Henry Suzzallo

title: Summer 1922: a full house
summary: The 1922 session enrolled 93 students from colleges in 11 states and two other countries (the centennial timeline counts 89), and the Swedish seaweed specialist Harald Kylin spent several weeks at the station. The launch Jestina carried classes out from the harbor, and at the season's close students strongly favored the planned move to the larger Point Caution site.

title: San Juan waters become a marine biological preserve
summary: The Washington legislature declared the salt waters, seabeds and shores of San Juan County and Cypress Island a marine biological preserve and made the station's director responsible for protecting it, with exceptions for harvesting food and for bull kelp. The law is still in force as RCW 28B.20.320.
sources: [{"title": "Mills & Hermans, FHL Historical Centennial Timeline (1923 entry, citing RCW 28B.20.320)", "url": "https://faculty.washington.edu/cemills/FHLTimeline.html"}]

title: Robert Moran gives the boat Rosario
summary: Shipbuilder Robert Moran of Rosario on Orcas Island gave the university his tow boat Rosario, worth about $12,000, for the biological station's use. The Regents thanked him for the gift and for his earlier offers to help set up the station at Point Caution.

title: Building begins at Point Caution
summary: A well drilled at the new site in 1922 reached 540 feet without giving enough water, so a pipeline was laid from the Friday Harbor town main, and in July 1923 the Regents set aside up to $22,000 for new buildings. By October two laboratories were going up, with materials barged in from Seattle, and the larger-than-usual 1923 session was the last held at the old Newhall site.
people: J. B. Hamilton; T. C. Frye

title: The new campus takes shape
summary: The first buildings at Point Caution were two stucco-and-tile laboratories (today's Labs 4 and 5), a dining hall designed by UW campus architect Carl F. Gould with a library at each end, and a caretaker's cottage finished in August 1924; the Regents had budgeted up to $22,000 for the first buildings, $25,000 for the dining hall and related work, and $3,000 for the cottage. Two more laboratories, today's Labs 2 and 3, were ready for the June 1925 session.

title: First summer on the present campus
summary: About 150 students and teachers came to the first session at Point Caution in 1924, after 104 tent platforms had been moved from the old site; meals were eaten outdoors until the dining hall was finished, the launch Justine was the research boat, and the Regents met at the station in July. UW's 2004 centennial release dates the move to 1923, but HistoryLink and the centennial timeline put the first classes there in 1924, and the Regents' minutes show the buildings still under construction in late 1923.

title: An art school planned for the old station
summary: With the biological station moving to Point Caution, the university's department of painting, sculpture and design announced a summer landscape-painting school under John Butler, to be held in the old station quarters in Friday Harbor.
sources: [{"title": "The Seattle Star, May 12, 1924, p. 8, 'New Art Center: Colony Planned for Friday Harbor by U' (Chronicling America)", "url": "https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn87093407/1924-05-12/ed-1/?sp=8"}]

title: Station research known abroad
summary: By 1925 the station's research filled three and a half published volumes, among them a guide to the marine shells of Puget Sound and a list of Washington's rust fungi. The UW yearbook said that exchanges of the series had made the station better known abroad than the university itself.
people: T. C. Frye; Ida Shepard Oldroyd; J. W. Hotson
sources: [{"title": "Tyee 1925 yearbook, profile of Professor Frye", "url": "https://digitalcollections.lib.washington.edu/digital/collection/uwdocs/id/15254"}]

title: Summer term stretched to nine weeks
summary: The Regents extended the station's summer term from six to nine weeks, in effect from 1926, and backed President Suzzallo's plan to seek foundation money for research laboratories and housing after he toured the station with Wickliffe Rose of the General Education Board. Attendance kept rising, to a record 210, including 150 students, in 1929.

title: Undergraduate George Hitchings studies Argyle Lagoon
summary: UW undergraduate George Hitchings worked with chemist Thomas G. Thompson on the seawater chemistry of Argyle Lagoon, and the work became his first scientific paper. Sixty-one years later he shared a Nobel Prize (see 1988).

title: Labs 1 and 6 and a lecture hall
summary: With today's Labs 1 and 6, a lecture hall and a director's cottage, the campus reached ten buildings, along with about 100 tents and some 20 rowboats. Frye told a local business club that the state had now put about $100,000 into the station.

title: Frye departs; chemist Thomas G. Thompson takes charge
summary: Frye resigned after a largely political struggle with chemist Thomas G. Thompson, who had secured Rockefeller Foundation backing for oceanography. Thompson became director, with Lyman Phifer as resident assistant director, and a new staff in oceanographic physics, chemistry, zoology and botany replaced the summer classes for schoolteachers that had defined the Frye years.
people: Thomas G. Thompson; T. C. Frye; Lyman Phifer; Clinton Utterback

title: The station becomes the UW Oceanographic Laboratories
summary: The biological station became the Friday Harbor field branch of UW's new Oceanographic Laboratories, alongside a main laboratory on the Seattle campus and a seagoing floating laboratory, a role filled from 1932 by the research ship Catalyst. Friday Harbor kept the Oceanographic Laboratories name until 1958.

title: A Rockefeller gift launches oceanography
summary: The Rockefeller Foundation gave UW $250,000 for oceanography, $200,000 for a laboratory building on the Seattle campus and $50,000 toward a research vessel, a grant its president recommended because of the work at Friday Harbor under Thompson. The Regents accepted it on January 17, 1931, and that March set aside a matching $50,000 to equip the oceanographic laboratories on campus and at Friday Harbor; the centennial timeline dates the grant to 1930.

title: The research ship Catalyst
summary: The 75-foot motorship Catalyst, built by Lake Union Drydock in Seattle with Rockefeller Foundation money, was launched in June 1932 as the laboratories' floating lab and left Friday Harbor that August on a research cruise to Alaska. In 1942 the university sold it to the Coast Guard for $28,500 for wartime service, including patrols in the Aleutians, and it never returned.

title: Mapping the seafloor communities
summary: Ecologist Victor E. Shelford, who first taught at the station in 1914, published a study of the seafloor animal communities of the San Juan Islands in Ecological Monographs. That summer about twice as many students came as in 1934, for courses on light in seawater, shipworms, marine bacteria and sea chemistry.

title: A deep-water dock and stone seawalls
summary: In March 1935 a 204-foot pier out to deep water replaced the beach-anchored floats in front of Lab 5, with one float for rowboats and another for keeping specimens alive. That October a Civilian Conservation Corps crew from Moran State Park built the stone bulkheads below the labs, which were repaired in 2007 and were still in use in 2010.
sources: [{"title": "Mills & Hermans, FHL Historical Centennial Timeline (1935 entries)", "url": "https://faculty.washington.edu/cemills/FHLTimeline.html"}]

title: Libbie Hyman returns
summary: Invertebrate zoologist Libbie Hyman, who had first come as a student at the old Warbass Way site, spent a second summer at Friday Harbor and ranked it above other American marine stations. Two years later she began publishing her six-volume treatise on invertebrate zoology.
sources: [{"title": "Mills & Hermans, FHL Historical Centennial Timeline (1938 entry)", "url": "https://faculty.washington.edu/cemills/FHLTimeline.html"}]

title: Wartime: the Coast Guard takes over
summary: Classes were suspended for World War II, and from August 22, 1942 the Coast Guard used the station under a wartime arrangement with the Regents to train recruits in groups of about 60, numbering the lab buildings 1 to 6 as barracks, as they still are. Assistant director Lyman Phifer and custodian John Dixon took Coast Guard commissions and stayed on, and the university at first paid Phifer to keep up its scientific readings there.

title: Dixy Lee Ray joins the zoology faculty
summary: Zoologist Dixy Lee Ray joined UW in 1945 and developed an introductory marine biology field course at Friday Harbor, and in the 1950s she presented marine biology on Seattle television, including a 1958 KCTS series filmed largely at the labs. She later chaired the Atomic Energy Commission, and as governor of Washington she spoke warmly of the labs when the Regents met there in 1977.

title: The station returns to the university
summary: The Coast Guard gave the station back to UW in early February 1946, and plant supervisor John Dixon came back to oversee repairs; the only class that summer was an archaeology field course on San Juan Island. Full summer teaching in botany, zoology and oceanography resumed in 1947, together with graduate work in meteorology.

title: Captain Vandersluys and the Hydah
summary: Captain Cleave Vandersluys bought the fishing boat Hydah in 1947, ferried books, equipment and students from Seattle that summer, and until 1983 collected specimens for classes and research, with several lab members learning the work as his deckhands. He learned scuba from Paul Sund in 1954, became the area's first commercial scuba diver and later supplied diving air to the labs; the Hydah was still the labs' research boat in 1974.

title: Cottages begin to replace the tent camp
summary: Director Thompson raised $10,000 to build ten year-round cottages, starting the shift away from the wood-and-canvas platform tents that had housed most summer residents; twelve tents were moved into the woods and student dormitories followed. A year earlier, San Juan County residents had offered to back a $325,000 state request for a laboratory, ten cabins and eighty tent platforms.

title: Labs and town start a fire department
summary: Friday Harbor and the labs set up a volunteer fire department together: the town supplied the firefighters and the labs a tank truck that Clifford Barnes got from government surplus and had rebuilt in UW shops. Students and faculty were already on call as volunteer firefighters in town.
sources: [{"title": "Mills & Hermans, FHL Historical Centennial Timeline (1947 and 1948 entries)", "url": "https://faculty.washington.edu/cemills/FHLTimeline.html"}]

title: Saved from closure
summary: The legislature cut the station's funding out of the university budget for 1950-51, and Arts and Sciences Dean Lloyd Woodburne kept it open by moving $20,000 from the athletics budget. After the near-closure the university reconsidered what the labs should become.
sources: [{"title": "Mills & Hermans, FHL Historical Centennial Timeline (1950-1951 entry)", "url": "https://faculty.washington.edu/cemills/FHLTimeline.html"}]

title: Experiments under the cantilever pier
summary: In the 1950s ecologist Joe Connell began long-term experiments on predators and prey among marine invertebrates on the seawall beneath the labs' cantilever pier, with parallel studies at Millport, Scotland. It was early work in the new field of experimental marine ecology.
sources: [{"title": "Mills & Hermans, FHL Historical Centennial Timeline (1950s entry)", "url": "https://faculty.washington.edu/cemills/FHLTimeline.html"}]

title: An all-glass seawater system
summary: Thompson obtained surplus industrial Pyrex pipe from Hanford and built an all-glass seawater system that replaced galvanized pipes carrying moderately toxic water, giving every lab running seawater free of metal contamination and opening new kinds of studies of living cells and organisms. The centennial timeline dates the system to 1950-51, and UW photographers recorded it as new in August 1952.
people: Thomas G. Thompson; Arthur H. Whiteley; Robert L. Fernald

title: Thompson retires; Richard Fleming leads
summary: After Thompson retired, Richard H. Fleming, co-author of the textbook The Oceans, came from Scripps to direct the Oceanographic Laboratories and to chair UW's new Oceanography Department. In 1956 he gave up the Friday Harbor post to concentrate on the department in Seattle, and after that oceanography and the island labs went separate ways.
people: Richard H. Fleming; Thomas G. Thompson

title: A blueprint for a year-round station
summary: A committee appointed by Dean Woodburne recommended that the labs operate all year, concentrate on marine science and on advanced teaching and research, and have a director with no other job. These recommendations shaped the modern station, and through the 1950s teaching was rebuilt around whole-organism biology, with UW faculty teaching alongside visitors from the US and abroad over a ten-week summer.
sources: [{"title": "Mills & Hermans, FHL Historical Centennial Timeline (1952 and 1950s entries)", "url": "https://faculty.washington.edu/cemills/FHLTimeline.html"}]

title: Paul Illg anchors invertebrate teaching
summary: Crustacean specialist Paul Illg, formerly curator of invertebrates at the Smithsonian, joined UW Zoology and for three decades taught invertebrate zoology at Friday Harbor most summers, often with invited European colleagues. A lectureship endowed in his name in 1998 brings a leading invertebrate biologist to the labs every year.

title: Scuba comes to marine research
summary: Graduate student Paul Sund became the first person to use scuba for research at the labs, first surveying animals and bottom types for an advanced invertebrate class and then diving for his own study of a sea anemone through 1956. By the late 1960s scuba studies of the subtidal zone were common in graduate theses done at the labs.

title: Renamed Friday Harbor Laboratories
summary: The station became the University of Washington Friday Harbor Laboratories. In May 1958 the Regents moved its administration and budget from the College of Arts and Sciences to the Graduate School, effective June 1, which made its separation from oceanography final.

title: Robert Fernald named director
summary: Zoologist Robert L. Fernald led the labs as acting director after Fleming stepped aside (from 1956 by the centennial timeline; the Regents approved his acting appointment in October 1958, effective that September), was named director effective April 1, 1960, and served until 1972. Starting with a permanent staff of one secretary and four maintenance workers, he recruited co-instructors from around the world and made comparative invertebrate embryology a strength of the labs.
people: Robert L. Fernald; Charles E. Odegaard

title: Jellyfish light: aequorin and GFP
summary: Osamu Shimomura and Frank Johnson of Princeton began making summer trips to Friday Harbor to collect large numbers of the glowing jellyfish Aequorea. In 1961-62 they purified from it aequorin, a protein that gives off light in the presence of calcium, and green fluorescent protein (GFP). Shimomura came back for about 20 summers through 1988, and both proteins became standard laboratory tools around the world.

title: The Main Lab opens
summary: A $350,000 National Science Foundation grant, accepted in 1960 on the understanding that the university would fund related housing and utilities through the state capital budget, paid for a central laboratory designed by Seattle architect Ralph Anderson; it opened in June 1962 with year-round lab space, a library, aquaria, a cold room and the director's office. Now called the Fernald Lab, it was the first modern building of the year-round station, built alongside new utilities and a maintenance building (1961-62), with a new dock and new housing coming later.

title: NSF support opens the doors to students
summary: Fernald won National Science Foundation grants, among them a $437,900 award in 1963 for facilities and marine research, that paid summer costs for most students and funded a resident postdoctoral researcher. When that money ran out, the FHL Marine Science Fund was set up so that students could be admitted on merit rather than ability to pay.

title: Beyond summer: spring courses
summary: Courses were added in spring quarter, an important step in turning the summer school into a place for teaching and research all year. Graduate students such as Mary E. Rice, who came to UW in 1961 and finished her PhD in 1966, were already among the first to work at the labs through the winter.

title: A resident associate director on the island
summary: Invertebrate zoologist Eugene Kozloff, who had first taught the summer invertebrate course in 1961, joined the UW faculty in 1966 and moved to Friday Harbor as the labs' first year-round resident associate director, at a time when the director worked mostly in Seattle. He held that post until 1973 and remained at the labs as a teacher and naturalist for decades.

title: Giant barnacles show how muscles are switched on
summary: Physiologist Graham Hoyle learned about the very large muscle cells of the local giant barnacle at a gathering at FHL with ecologist Joe Connell; accounts date it to 1960 or 1963. In 1967 Ellis Ridgway and Chris Ashley used those fibers and Shimomura's aequorin to show that calcium ions control muscle contraction, and barnacle muscle became a widely used model for studying how muscles, including the heart, work.

title: Dennis Willows begins a 33-year directorship
summary: The Regents appointed neurobiologist A. O. Dennis Willows director from December 16, 1972, succeeding Fernald. Willows had first worked at the labs as a University of Oregon graduate student in 1963 or 1964, and in 1967 he published a Science paper linking a sea slug's behavior to a single brain cell. He led FHL until 2005, the longest directorship in its history.

title: Zoobot: a full quarter for undergraduates
summary: Eugene Kozloff and phycologist Richard Norris taught the first 'Zoobot' spring quarter, a full-time program in marine invertebrate zoology and seaweed biology, mainly for undergraduates from the Seattle campus, and it was offered at least once a year for more than 35 years. In the same year larval biologist Richard Strathmann became resident associate director, a post he held until 2008.

title: False Bay tidelands bought for research
summary: The Regents bought about 250 acres of False Bay tidelands on San Juan Island and about 21 acres of adjoining upland for $150,000, with Director Willows at the meeting to describe the area's research uses. The wide tidal flats, where students had been collecting since at least 1913, became one of the labs' biological preserves.

title: Shaw Island land for the labs
summary: Frederick E. and Marilyn S. Ellis gave the university about 355 acres on western Shaw Island, with some 1,500 feet of waterfront, to be kept in its natural state as a scientific preserve, following Frederick Ellis's 1969 gift of about 26 acres at Point George for the labs' use. More Point George land from him followed in 1981-82, under restrictions keeping it permanently as a wildlife preserve used only for research.

title: The first biomechanics course
summary: Stephen Wainwright, who helped bring comparative biomechanics to FHL and to the wider world, taught FHL's first summer biomechanics course with Steven Vogel and Mimi Koehl. Students from around the world took these courses and many became leaders in the field, and several later FHL faculty count as products of them.

title: A floating breakwater for year-round work
summary: An L-shaped concrete floating breakwater was anchored off the station's shore, about half a mile north of the Port of Friday Harbor, so that marine research work could continue all year. It also served as a staging area for nets and gear and as sheltered mooring.

title: Cedar Rock Preserve enlarged
summary: A bequest from the estate of Robert Hale Ellis Jr. added about 114 acres of Shaw Island, with more than 2,000 feet of shoreline, to the Cedar Rock Preserve, to be kept as a nature preserve under the FHL director. With Point Caution, False Bay, Argyle Lagoon and other sites, it became part of more than 1,500 acres of preserves managed by the labs.

title: A station alumnus wins the Nobel Prize
summary: George Hitchings, who did his first research, on the chemistry of seawater, at the station as a UW undergraduate in 1927, shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. A 2008 FHL newsletter counted him as the first of two Nobel laureates who had worked summers at the labs, the second being Osamu Shimomura.

title: Fall courses from the East-West program
summary: Northeastern University's East-West Marine Biology Program, then led by Ken Sebens, who later became FHL's director, taught fall courses at the labs from 1990 to 2003.

title: Marine reserves in the San Juans
summary: Marine preserves were established in the San Juan Archipelago in 1990, and four of them, beside the labs' land preserves, came to be managed jointly by FHL and the state Department of Fish and Wildlife. By 2008 the FHL director reported that lingcod had recovered sharply in numbers and size inside them and that several rockfish species were more abundant than at comparison sites, a change not seen in the county's voluntary bottomfish zones.

title: An advisory board of alumni and friends
summary: Director Dennis Willows founded what became the FHL Advancement Board, a volunteer group of alumni and friends who raise private money for students, postdocs and new projects; one newsletter's count would place its start in 1996. Its fundraising created many endowments and the Adopt-a-Student program, and together with a UW campaign it helped raise more than $10 million in the 2010s.

summary: With support from the UW Provost, FHL started its Research Apprenticeship Program in spring 1999, in which small teams of undergraduates spend a whole academic quarter at the labs doing real research with faculty. In 2002 it won UW's Brotman Award for collaborative teaching and gained support from a $2.2 million Howard Hughes Medical Institute grant to UW biology, and by 2008 more than 400 students had taken part.

title: R/V Centennial joins the fleet
summary: FHL bought a 58-foot steel trawler built in 1990 for the Alaska fisheries, converted it for research in Everett, and named it Centennial in honor of the labs' approaching 100th anniversary. It was used for trawling, dredging, plankton and water sampling and class trips until it was retired in summer 2019 and replaced by the smaller R/V Kittiwake, which is cheaper to run.

title: The Center for Cell Dynamics
summary: With a five-year, $10.7 million NIH grant, the Center for Cell Dynamics opened at FHL in autumn 2002 under Garrett Odell as the first of seven national centers for systems biology, combining computer simulation with microscope studies of marine embryos and cells. Its 5,040-square-foot building, Lab 10, was finished in April 2004 and kept the campus active through the winters.

title: One hundred years
summary: UW leaders and guests gathered at the labs on July 17, 2004, to mark 100 years since the first summer session, partway through a series of six centennial symposia held from 2003 to 2005; FHL then had nine research labs and more than 1,500 acres of preserves. One symposium, on light-producing and fluorescent proteins, brought together Osamu Shimomura, Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien, who shared a Nobel Prize four years later.

title: Endowing the core courses
summary: Concerned that basic field courses were disappearing nationwide, Dennis Willows and Betsy Gladfelter started the Marine Life Endowment to secure FHL's core summer courses on invertebrates, algae, fishes and embryology, which had been taught almost every year since 1904. Within nine months alumni and friends pledged over 70% of the $4.5 million goal, and by 2008 the campaign had met its target, mostly through bequests worth more than $7 million.

title: A Nobel Prize rooted in Friday Harbor jellyfish
summary: Osamu Shimomura shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien for green fluorescent protein, which came from Aequorea jellyfish he collected in Friday Harbor during about 20 summers at the labs between 1961 and 1988; he was the second Nobel laureate with ties to FHL. By then Aequorea and most of the region's other jellyfish had become rare in local waters, for reasons that are not known.

summary: FHL started its first regular autumn program, the Marine Biology Quarter, which let undergraduates live at the labs for a whole term. Its four courses, among them the labs' first scientific diving course, counted toward UW's new marine biology minor, and the program kept growing, with its largest group yet in 2011.

summary: An NSF grant led by Adam Summers and Emily Carrington made FHL a Research Experiences for Undergraduates site, building on fellowships for students from diverse backgrounds that John Blinks had funded in 1996, and the first combined group of twelve undergraduates arrived in summer 2010. title: An ocean acidification laboratory
summary: Following a 2009 NSF award, and with NSF, UW and private money, FHL finished a 1,500-square-foot ocean acidification laboratory in spring 2011, equipped for carbonate chemistry, with more than 100 CO2-controlled aquaria and experimental enclosures moored off the dock; its first enclosure experiment ran that June. That summer FHL also taught what it described as the country's first graduate course in ocean acidification methods, and the lab became part of the new Center for the Ecology of Changing Oceans.

title: Sea star wasting disease
summary: Starting in 2013, a wasting disease killed billions of sea stars along the Pacific coast, among them ochre stars and sunflower stars, which had once been a common sight on the labs' dock pilings. Cornell's Drew Harvell and others studied the epidemic from FHL, and tank experiments there found that infected adult stars died faster in warmer water.

summary: Developmental biologist Billie J. Swalla, who had worked at FHL since 1999 and served as acting or interim director since 2012, was named director in August 2014, the first woman in the job. summary: FHL raised roughly $300,000 to $340,000 in private and UW funds for a CT scanner, which arrived in late 2015 and anchors its Karel F. Liem imaging facility, and Adam Summers launched #ScanAllFishes to put free 3D scans of fish species online; by 2024 the labs had scanned more than 7,200 specimens for the open oVert project. summary: Working with the SeaDoc Society and OceanGate, FHL scientists and students made research dives in the five-person submersible Cyclops 1, the first crewed submersible to work in the San Juans, studying sand lance, a trawl site long used in teaching, and red sea urchins. summary: After wasting disease had wiped out most sunflower stars, Jason Hodin's team kept wild adults in FHL's seawater tanks and achieved the first successful spawning of the species, which began a breeding program with The Nature Conservancy. By spring 2021 the larvae had become juveniles no bigger than poppy seeds, and by 2022 about 900 were growing in the labs' tanks.

summary: When UW moved online in March 2020, FHL kept only essential staff on site, cancelled all but two spring courses, closed the grounds to visitors and called off its open house. summary: In late June 2021 extreme heat arrived during the year's lowest tides, which on inland shores fell around midday, and killed shellfish on beaches in the Salish Sea and along the outer coast. FHL research scientist Wendel Raymond led the study that reconstructed the die-off.

summary: In 2023 FHL offered a course on the Indigenous history of the Salish Sea, hosted an inter-tribal canoe family and let a Coast Salish youth canoe group camp on its Shaw Island land, and carvers from the Williams family restored a donated Nuu-chah-nulth totem pole in the entry of the Fernald Lab. summary: With nearly $400,000 from NSF, awarded in 2022, FHL's own crew rebuilt and re-equipped Lab 2, one of the 1925 laboratories, and it opened in June 2024 as the Marine Genomics Center; a public opening followed on May 1, 2025. In summer 2025 an international workshop there sequenced environmental DNA from seawater on site and detected more than 700 species.

title: First lab-raised sunflower stars return to the sea
summary: Divers put 20 FHL-bred sunflower stars, one to three years old, into an eelgrass meadow off the labs' dock, the first captive-bred members of the species to be returned to the wild; a month earlier the lab had hosted its first Echinoderm Academy, a workshop teaching researchers and zoo and aquarium staff how to breed them. The team went on to plan further releases to study whether the stars can curb growing sea urchin populations that threaten kelp.

title: Lean times and an aging waterfront
summary: With a Washington state budget deficit and federal research funding uncertain, FHL cut its core budget by 5% without layoffs, leaned more on donor endowments, and held off on expanding, including the center on climate solutions and marine species recovery it had proposed in 2024. Its December 2025 Tide Bite listed waterfront needs that included a new dock crane (about $80,000) and a new research vessel (about $4 million).

title: The cause of sea star wasting is found
summary: A study led by the Hakai Institute and the University of British Columbia, with FHL-affiliated scientists Drew Harvell and Jason Hodin among the collaborators, identified a strain of the bacterium Vibrio pectenicida as a cause of sea star wasting disease. Sunflower stars raised in Hodin's FHL lab were used as test animals, and the key strain, FHCF-3, has 'FH' in its name for Friday Harbor.

title: The campus today
summary: FHL's December 2025 newsletter mapped how its labs are used: Lab 1 is the hub of sunflower star recovery work, Lab 2 holds genomics, Lab 6 the flow flumes and a wind tunnel, Lab 8 fish research and the Liem imaging facility, Lab 10 (formerly the Center for Cell Dynamics) genomics and insect neurodevelopment, and Lab 12 ocean acidification research. Several of the wet labs date from the 1920s and, the labs noted in 2022, had been only partly remodeled in the 1980s.

title: Sunflower stars released with the Samish Indian Nation
summary: Twenty three-year-old sunflower stars raised at FHL were released into a cove off Decatur Island in partnership with the Samish Indian Nation. A release planned for October 2025 had been postponed after wasting disease broke out again.
